column1: What two things must an ordinary induction proof establish?
column2: Base case: P(0). Inductive step: P(n) ⇒ P(n+1) for every n ≥ 0.

column1: In the inductive step, what are you allowed to assume, and what must you show?
column2: Assume P(n) for an arbitrary n; show P(n+1). You prove the implication, not P(n) itself.

column1: The five parts of an induction proof (MCS template)
column2: 1. Say it's induction. 2. Define P(n) explicitly. 3. Base case. 4. Inductive step for all n. 5. Conclude.

column1: Courtyard tiling: why does 'Bill in the centre' fail as the induction hypothesis?
column2: After splitting into quadrants, Bill sits at a quadrant corner, not its centre, so P(n) says nothing about the pieces.

column1: What is 'strengthening the induction hypothesis' and why does it help?
column2: Prove a stronger P(n), e.g. 'Bill anywhere'. You have more to prove, but you also get to assume more in the inductive step.

column1: Where does the 'all horses are the same colour' proof break?
column2: The inductive step fails at n = 1: two sets of one horse each don't overlap, so nothing links them.

column1: How does induction show that a recursive function is correct?
column2: Base case = the base case of the recursion. Inductive step = assume the recursive call returns the right answer, then show this call does.
